persona.name: Deepak Joshi
persona.background: Deepak helps run his family’s small shop in Indore and lives in a crowded neighborhood where skin infections are common among children in the household.

diagnoses.name: Poststreptococcal (postinfectious) glomerulonephritis
diagnoses.description: An immune complex–mediated acute proliferative glomerulonephritis occurring after a latent period of 1–4 weeks following streptococcal pharyngitis or skin infection; a common cause of acute nephritic syndrome in children 6–10 years.

diagnoses.name: IgA nephropathy
diagnoses.description: A glomerular disease that can present with microscopic or recurrent episodes of macroscopic hematuria following upper respiratory infection.

diagnoses.name: Lupus nephritis
diagnoses.description: Renal involvement in systemic lupus erythematosus characterized by proteinuria, hematuria, and cellular (red and white blood cell) casts; low complement (C3) may indicate active nephritis.

diagnoses.name: Acute tubulointerstitial nephropathy (acute interstitial nephritis)
diagnoses.description: An inflammatory condition affecting renal tubules and interstitium, commonly due to drugs/toxins or infections, with tubular dysfunction, moderate proteinuria, and varying degrees of renal impairment.

diagnoses.name: Acute nephritic syndrome
diagnoses.description: Syndrome characterized by hematuria (gross or microscopic), red cell casts, azotemia (temporary), temporary oliguria (due to decreased GFR), hypertension, proteinuria, and edema (not as severe as nephrotic syndrome).

diagnoses.name: Minimal change disease
diagnoses.description: A primary cause of nephrotic syndrome in children, with massive proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, generalized edema, hyperlipidemia and lipiduria; RBCs and red cell casts are not seen in minimal change disease.

diagnoses.name: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS)
diagnoses.description: A cause of nephrotic syndrome usually manifesting with nephrotic syndrome or heavy proteinuria, hypertension, renal insufficiency, and occasionally hematuria.

diagnoses.name: Membranous nephropathy
diagnoses.description: A common adult cause of nephrotic syndrome with diffuse capillary wall thickening; about 75% present with nephrotic-range proteinuria and 50% with microscopic hematuria.

diagnoses.name: Chronic kidney disease (CKD)
diagnoses.description: Progressive kidney dysfunction where urinalysis may show fixed specific gravity around 1.010 (isosthenuria), hematuria or proteinuria; broad casts may be seen, and complications include anemia and hypertension.

diagnoses.name: Urinary tract infection (acute cystitis/pyelonephritis spectrum)
diagnoses.description: Infection defined by bacteriuria (>10^5 organism/mL in MSU); symptomatic disease includes lower UTI (cystitis/urethritis/prostatitis) and upper UTI (acute pyelonephritis).

precomputedExplanations.description: **Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN)** is an immune-mediated **glomerulonephritis** that occurs after a latent period following **group A streptococcal** throat or skin infection. Immune complex deposition activates **complement**, causing acute **nephritic syndrome** with hematuria, edema, hypertension, and transient azotemia.
keySymptoms: **Cola-colored urine (gross hematuria)** - Indicates glomerular bleeding; classic nephritic sign after recent streptococcal infection latency.
**Periorbital/facial edema** - Reflects salt and water retention from reduced GFR and renal inflammation.
**Oliguria (reduced urine output)** - Suggests decreased glomerular filtration from acute inflammatory glomerular injury.
**Hypertension** - Due to volume expansion and activation of pressor mechanisms during acute nephritic syndrome.
**Azotemia (elevated urea/creatinine)** - Demonstrates transient reduction in kidney function consistent with acute nephritic syndrome.
**Red cell casts on urinalysis** - Highly suggestive of glomerulonephritis; RBCs originate from inflamed glomeruli.
**Proteinuria** - Occurs from increased glomerular permeability; usually subnephrotic in nephritic syndromes.
precomputedExplanations.clinicalReasoning: An 8-year-old with abrupt **cola-colored urine**, **periorbital edema**, **oliguria**, and **hypertension** fits an acute **nephritic syndrome** pattern. Urinalysis showing **hematuria with red cell casts** localizes bleeding to the glomerulus, supporting **glomerulonephritis** rather than lower-tract causes. The history of a latent period after likely streptococcal skin infection plus expected immunology (often **low complement** and elevated **ASO/anti-DNase B**) strongly supports **PSGN**. Classic pathology would show diffuse endocapillary inflammation with neutrophils and **IgG/C3** deposition, with subepithelial electron-dense “humps” on EM.

**Hypertension** - May occur with progressive disease or during active nephritic episodes.
**Flank discomfort** - Sometimes present during episodes of hematuria, especially in older children/adolescents.

**Hypertension** - Volume expansion and RAAS activation elevate blood pressure during acute glomerular inflammation.
**Oliguria** - Reduced urine output reflects decreased GFR from inflamed, obstructed glomerular capillary loops.
**Azotemia** - Elevated urea/creatinine occurs when acute glomerular injury reduces filtration temporarily.

**Long-standing growth failure** - Chronic pediatric CKD often presents with poor growth over time; not indicated here.

precomputedExplanations.description: A **urinary tract infection (UTI)** is a bacterial infection of the bladder (**cystitis**) or kidneys (**pyelonephritis**). It typically causes irritative voiding symptoms and/or systemic signs of infection, and urinalysis classically shows **pyuria** and **bacteriuria** rather than glomerular findings.
keySymptoms: **Dysuria** - Burning or pain with urination due to inflamed bladder/urethral mucosa from infection.
**Urinary frequency/urgency** - Frequent small voids and urgent need to urinate from bladder irritation.
**Suprapubic pain** - Lower abdominal discomfort typical of **cystitis** from bladder wall inflammation.
**Fever** - Suggests upper-tract involvement (**pyelonephritis**) or systemic inflammatory response.
**Flank pain/CVA tenderness** - Kidney involvement causing pain at costovertebral angle with **pyelonephritis**.
**Pyuria** - White blood cells in urine reflecting infection-driven inflammation in the urinary tract.
**Positive nitrites/leukocyte esterase** - Dipstick evidence of gram-negative bacteria and WBC activity in urine.
precomputedExplanations.clinicalReasoning: UTI is considered when a child has urinary symptoms (dysuria, frequency), fever, and urinalysis showing **pyuria** and **bacteriuria**. Hematuria can occur in UTI, but it is usually microscopic and not accompanied by **red cell casts**, which indicate a glomerular source. Hypertension, periorbital edema, oliguria, and azotemia point toward an **acute nephritic syndrome** rather than a lower urinary tract infection. The described latent period after a likely streptococcal skin infection further supports a postinfectious immune process, not an ascending bacterial UTI.
precomputedExplanations.whyIncorrectForCase: This patient has **cola-colored urine**, **periorbital edema**, **hypertension**, **azotemia**, and **red cell casts**, which strongly indicate **glomerulonephritis** rather than UTI. UTI would more typically present with **dysuria**, **frequency**, **fever**, and urinalysis dominated by **pyuria/bacteriuria**, not glomerular casts.
keyDifferencesFromCorrect: **Urine sediment** - UTI shows **pyuria** and bacteria; PSGN shows **hematuria with red cell casts**.
**Pathophysiology** - UTI is direct bacterial infection; PSGN is **immune complex–mediated** glomerular injury after streptococcal infection.
**Blood pressure/edema** - UTI usually lacks **hypertension** and **periorbital edema**; PSGN commonly has both.
**Complement levels** - UTI does not cause **low complement**; PSGN often has **low C3** from complement consumption.
**Timing** - UTI symptoms occur during active infection; PSGN follows a **latent period** after streptococcal skin/throat infection.
missingFindings: **Pyuria** - Absence of prominent WBCs argues against an infectious cystitis/pyelonephritis pattern.
**Bacteriuria/positive urine culture** - Lack of bacterial growth would not support UTI as the primary diagnosis.
**Nitrites/leukocyte esterase positivity** - If negative, it reduces likelihood of typical gram-negative UTI.
**Dysuria/frequency/urgency** - Missing irritative voiding symptoms makes lower UTI less likely.
**Fever and flank pain** - Absence of systemic/upper-tract signs weakens pyelonephritis consideration.

keyHistoryQuestions.action: Ask about recent sore throat (pharyngitis) or skin infection (impetigo/pyoderma) in the last 1–4 weeks
keyHistoryQuestions.reasoning: PSGN typically follows a primary streptococcal infection after a latent period compatible with antibody production and immune complex formation.
keyHistoryQuestions.expectedFinding: History of sore throat recovery or recent impetigo/pyoderma occurring 1–4 weeks before onset of cola-colored urine/oliguria/edema
keyHistoryQuestions.textbookReference: “It manifests usually after a latent period of 1–4 weeks following primary streptococcal infection.”

keyHistoryQuestions.action: Ask about hematuria characteristics (smoky/red/cola-colored urine) and onset (abrupt)
keyHistoryQuestions.reasoning: Hematuria with characteristic urine color and abrupt onset is a key clinical feature of PSGN/acute nephritic syndrome.
keyHistoryQuestions.textbookReference: “Onset is often abrupt… hematuria (characteristically, urine appears smoky or red or cola-colored urine)”

keyHistoryQuestions.reasoning: Temporary oliguria is part of acute nephritic syndrome and is specifically listed among PSGN urinary findings.
keyHistoryQuestions.textbookReference: “Temporary oliguria (due to decreased glomerular filtration rate)”

keyHistoryQuestions.action: Ask about edema distribution and progression (periorbital puffiness, dependent edema; possible ascites/pleural effusion)
keyHistoryQuestions.reasoning: Edema (often periorbital initially) is a typical presenting feature in PSGN.
keyHistoryQuestions.expectedFinding: Periorbital puffiness progressing to dependent edema; may be associated with ascites and/or pleural effusion
keyHistoryQuestions.textbookReference: “Periorbital edema… Edema initially appears in areas of low tissue pressure (periorbital areas)… may be associated with ascites and/or pleural effusion.”

keyHistoryQuestions.action: Ask about systemic symptoms at onset (malaise, fever, nausea)
keyHistoryQuestions.reasoning: These symptoms are described as common at presentation in affected children.
keyHistoryQuestions.expectedFinding: Malaise and/or fever and/or nausea accompanying hematuria/oliguria
keyHistoryQuestions.textbookReference: “Usually the affected child suddenly develops malaise, fever, nausea, oliguria, and hematuria…”

keyExaminations.action: Measure blood pressure to assess for mild to moderate hypertension
keyExaminations.reasoning: Hypertension is a characteristic feature of acute nephritic syndrome and is commonly observed in PSGN.
keyExaminations.textbookReference: “mild to moderate hypertension is usually observed.”

keyExaminations.action: Examine for edema, especially periorbital puffiness and dependent edema
keyExaminations.reasoning: Edema is a key sign of PSGN and part of acute nephritic syndrome.

keyExaminations.action: Assess volume overload complications clinically (look for features consistent with pulmonary edema)
keyExaminations.reasoning: Pulmonary edema is listed as a complication of acute PSGN/nephritic syndrome and should be actively looked for in symptomatic patients.
keyExaminations.expectedFinding: Clinical evidence suggesting pulmonary edema (if present as a complication)

keyInvestigations.action: Order urinalysis with urine microscopy to look for hematuria and red cell casts
keyInvestigations.reasoning: Acute nephritic syndrome/PSGN is characterized by hematuria with RBC casts; urine microscopy may show dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts.
keyInvestigations.expectedFinding: Hematuria with dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts; mild proteinuria
keyInvestigations.textbookReference: “Urine microscopy: – Red cells (particularly dysmorphic…) – Red cell casts”

keyInvestigations.reasoning: Renal impairment may occur in PSGN and is reflected by elevated urea and creatinine.
keyInvestigations.expectedFinding: Urea and creatinine may be elevated indicating renal impairment
keyInvestigations.textbookReference: “Urea and creatinine: May be elevated and indicates renal impairment”

keyInvestigations.action: Order serum complement levels (C3; complement components)
keyInvestigations.reasoning: More than 90% of PSGN patients have hypocomplementemia; complement helps differentiate nephritic syndromes (low vs normal complement).
keyInvestigations.expectedFinding: Significant reduction in serum concentration of complement (C3) components
keyInvestigations.textbookReference: “more than 90% of patients reveal decreased complement (C3 and C4) levels… (hypocomplementemia).”

keyInvestigations.action: Order antistreptococcal antibody titers (e.g., ASO; consider anti-DNase B per available testing)
keyInvestigations.reasoning: Majority of patients show increased titers of antibodies against streptococcal antigens; Table 10.18 lists raised ASO titer.
keyInvestigations.expectedFinding: Raised antistreptococcal antibody titers (e.g., raised ASO titer)
keyInvestigations.textbookReference: “Raised antistreptococcal antibody, titers, e.g., antistreptolysin O (ASO) titer”

keyInvestigations.action: Consider renal biopsy if indicated to establish diagnosis or if atypical course/concern for RPGN-like presentation
keyInvestigations.reasoning: Renal biopsy in PSGN shows diffuse acute inflammation with neutrophils and deposition of IgG and complement; biopsy is indicated in nephritic syndrome when presentation is RPGN-like or if complement/hematuria abnormalities persist.
keyInvestigations.expectedFinding: Diffuse acute inflammation in glomerulus with neutrophils and deposition of IgG and complement; EM: electron-dense subepithelial deposits
keyInvestigations.textbookReference: “Renal biopsy: Diffuse acute inflammation… deposition of immunoglobulin G (IgG) and complement… electron-dense deposits in the subepithelial aspects…”

differentialDiagnoses.name: IgA nephropathy
differentialDiagnoses.howToRuleOut: Use complement levels in nephritic syndrome: IgA nephropathy is listed under normal complement, whereas PSGN is under low complement.
differentialDiagnoses.textbookReference: “Complement levels in nephritic syndrome… Low complement: Postinfectious glomerulonephritis… Normal complement: IgA nephropathy”

differentialDiagnoses.name: Lupus nephritis
differentialDiagnoses.howToRuleOut: Use complement levels: lupus nephritis is listed under low complement, so low complement alone does not distinguish; consider that PSGN is supported by raised antistreptococcal antibody titers and typical post-streptococcal latent period history.

differentialDiagnoses.name: Henoch–Schönlein purpura (HSP)
differentialDiagnoses.howToRuleOut: Use complement levels in nephritic syndrome: HSP is listed under low complement; PSGN is supported by evidence of preceding streptococcal infection (raised ASO/other antistreptococcal antibodies) and typical latent period.

differentialDiagnoses.name: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN)
differentialDiagnoses.howToRuleOut: Suspect if there is severe oliguria with rapid progressive loss of renal function; confirm with renal biopsy showing crescents. PSGN can be complicated by RPGN.
differentialDiagnoses.textbookReference: “Rapidly progressive loss of renal function… associated with severe oliguria… Renal biopsy: Shows crescents.”

idealPathway.diagnosticApproach: In a child presenting with abrupt cola-colored urine and facial puffiness, first confirm acute nephritic syndrome clinically (hematuria, edema, hypertension, oliguria). Elicit history of preceding streptococcal pharyngitis or skin infection with a 1–4 week latent period. Perform focused examination for blood pressure and edema. Order cost-effective tests first: urinalysis/urine microscopy for dysmorphic RBCs and red cell casts with mild proteinuria, then serum urea/creatinine for renal impairment. Next, support PSGN etiology with low complement (C3) and raised antistreptococcal antibody titers (e.g., ASO). Differentiate from other nephritic syndromes using complement patterns (PSGN typically low complement; IgA nephropathy normal complement). Consider renal biopsy to establish diagnosis in atypical cases or if an RPGN-like presentation is suspected, where biopsy would show crescents; in PSGN biopsy shows diffuse acute inflammation with neutrophils and IgG/complement deposition with subepithelial electron-dense deposits.
